findings.description: `baseUrl` is read from the session's tsconfig, has no length limit (only `readPlainFile`'s 1 MiB), and is left out of the new 2048-character count. `join(baseUrl, t)` puts a copy of it into every substitution. So a tsconfig with a ~1 MiB `baseUrl` and `"*": ["*" x 8]` passes all three bounds (entries 9, characters 9, substitutions 8). Every bare import then builds 8 targets of about 1 MiB each, roughly 136 strings of 1 MiB per import. That is the stall the round was meant to close, made worse.
findings.body:
**The new characters bound leaves out `baseUrl`, and `baseUrl` ends up in every candidate path. So the merge-lock stall is still reachable.**

`baseUrl` comes from the same session-controlled `compilerOptions` (`readPathAliases(ctx.measurePath)` reads the measured checkout's tsconfig). Its length is limited only by `readPlainFile`'s 1 MiB cap. L105 destructures it with no check, L107-112 count only pattern keys and targets, and L119 prepends it to every target with `join(baseUrl, t)`:

https://github.com/AlexisBalayre/pupitre/blob/23d9b71d0fc37b1a56d48464a00e89c6ebfe0384/src/adapters/typescript-source.utils.ts#L105-L119

This tsconfig passes all three bounds (entries = 9, chars = 9, substitutions = 8):

```json
{"compilerOptions":{"baseUrl":"xxxx…(~1,040,000 chars)","paths":{"*":["*","*","*","*","*","*","*","*"]}}}
```

`path.join` only collapses `.`/`..` segments and repeated slashes, so each target stays about 1 MiB long. `*` matches every bare import, including `node:*` and `vitest`. For each one:
- `aliasTargets` builds 8 copies of about 1 MiB each (L145).
- `resolveImport` maps all of them eagerly before `.find` (L168).
- `resolveFile` normalizes each one, then builds and hashes about 17 candidates per target (L171-181). A `baseUrl` that doesn't start with `..` never takes the early return.

That comes to about 136 strings of 1 MiB per import. `findDeadExports` calls this for every import, and `runMergeGate` runs the gate inside `withMergeLock` (`merge-gate.service.ts` ~L950). The cost is in the same range as the 255 × 4 KiB case the ADR measured at about 50 ms per import, or worse. So the JSDoc's "Characters cap the length of every string built from a substitution" and ADR 0130's "caps the length of each candidate path" / "worst measured case is about 0.1 ms per import" don't hold while `baseUrl` stays out of the count.

**Suggested fix:** count the explicit `baseUrl` in `chars`. A non-string `baseUrl` still ends in a throw from `join`, and the caller catches it.

```ts
const chars = entries.reduce(
  (n, [p, targets]) => n + p.length + targets.join('').length,
  (config.compilerOptions?.baseUrl ?? '').length,
);
```

Seeding with the explicit value keeps the existing 2048/2049 boundary test valid. Seeding with the defaulted `baseUrl.length` would add 1 for `'.'` and break that test. Add a case such as `{ baseUrl: 'x'.repeat(2048), paths: { '@a/*': ['*'] } }` → no aliases.

The timings are scaled from the ADR's own measurement. Nothing was run under CI.

findings.description: The specifier side has no bound, and its cost grows with source size rather than being a fixed amount per import. `aliasTargets` copies the matched part of the specifier into each of up to 8 targets, and each target then becomes about 17 candidate strings. A specifier of length L therefore costs about 136·L of string work, where a relative import costs about 17·L. Source files are read with `readFileSync` and no size cap (`typescript.adapter.ts` L91), but every byte of specifier is also a byte of source that `ts.createSourceFile` already parses. So this only multiplies an existing linear cost, by about 8x; it does not create a fixed-cost stall like finding 1. Even so, the ADR's "worst measured case is about 0.1 ms per import" (ADR 0130 L48-49) only holds for short specifiers, and the JSDoc's "Characters cap the length of every string built from a substitution" likewise ignores the matched specifier. Changing those to "per short import", or noting that the cost still grows with specifier length, would make the claims accurate.

A 2048-character cap over the whole `paths` drops all aliases for a moderately sized monorepo that declares its library aliases in the root `tsconfig.json`. A typical entry such as `"@acme/feature-billing": ["libs/feature/billing/src/index.ts"]` is about 54 characters, so the cap trips at about 38 aliases. The 256-entry cap alone allowed 128. Past that point the dead-export check silently goes back to relative-only resolution and reports every alias-only-imported export as dead. A per-string cap (longest pattern or substitution plus `baseUrl`) would bound candidate length the same way without counting the number of aliases twice, since the entry cap already limits that.

The ADR's *Bound.* paragraph repeats the JSDoc's "each bound caps one term" breakdown almost sentence for sentence, tells the debugging story twice ("The entry cap alone was not enough…" / "A characters cap alone was not enough either…"), and tags "(CI review, PR #218)" twice. Keep the measurements that justify the numbers, leave the mechanism to the JSDoc next to the code, and keep one tag.
